```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, dpi = 150)

library(repro)
# load the packages listed in the YAML header
automate_load_packages()
# register the external script(s) listed in the YAML header
automate_load_scripts()
# read the data file listed in the YAML header into an object named `raw`
raw <- automate_load_data(raw, read.csv)
```

# Overview

This document is part of the Open Materials accompanying the book chapter

> Brandmaier, A. M. (in press). Reproducible Workflows for Intensive Longitudinal Data Analysis in R. In T. Koch, T. Lischetzke, & J. Holtmann (Eds.),
> *Handbook of intensive longitudinal data analysis*. Routledge.

**Goal.** Demonstrate tools for reproducible research workflows with intensive
longitudinal data. We

1. recreate a panel from Figure 1 of Kossakowski et al. (2017),
2. fit a linear model for the time trend in the weekly depression ratings, and
3. use the `cocoon` package to write the model statistics **directly into the
   running text**.

**Caveat.** The study has several phases, which are *not* modeled here. The
analysis only illustrates the workflow; we draw no substantive conclusions.

## How this document is wired up

The YAML header of this file contains a `repro:` block that declares

- the **packages** the analysis needs (GitHub packages pinned to a commit),
- the **script** with the analysis code (`R/analysis.R`), and
- the **data** file (`data/ESMdata.csv`).

`repro::automate()` reads this block and generates a `Dockerfile` (the
environment) and a `Makefile` rule (the build recipe) from it. The analysis
code itself lives in `R/analysis.R`; the empty chunks below pull it in by
name, so the script and this report can never diverge. To reproduce the whole
report on any machine with `make` and Docker (R is not needed):

```
make docker            # build the image once
make all DOCKER=TRUE   # render this document inside the container
```

## Data

Data from Kossakowski, Groot, Haslbeck, Borsboom, and Wichers (2017; *Journal of
Open Psychology Data, 5*(1), [doi:10.5334/jopd.29](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.29);
OSF: <https://osf.io/j4fg8>; CC BY 4.0). It is a single-case (N = 1)
experience-sampling study with about 10 beeps per day over 239 days and 50
items. The participant is male, aged 57, has a history of multiple episodes of
major depression, and had used antidepressants for the previous 8.5 years. He
monitored his momentary experiential states during a gradual discontinuation of
his antidepressant. Depressive symptoms were additionally assessed **weekly**
with the SCL-90-R depression subscale (variable `dep`).

The data object `raw` was loaded in the setup chunk from the path given in the
YAML header: it contains `r nrow(raw)` rows (beeps).

# Preprocessing

The code for this section is the chunk `preprocess` in `R/analysis.R`: it
parses and checks the dates, sorts by date and beep number, adds a day counter,
and creates `beeps`, in which the weekly rating is carried forward to all
following beeps (used for plotting).

```{r preprocess}
```

The weekly rating is only recorded once per week. The model needs **one row per
actual weekly assessment**, which must be derived from the *unfilled* data
(otherwise carried-forward values leak into the first row of each week):

```{r weekly}
```

There are `r nrow(weekly)` weekly depression assessments.

# Plot

The figure recreates the SCL-90-R depression subscale panel of Figure 1a in
Kossakowski et al. (2017). The dashed line is the linear trend of the weekly
ratings.

```{r plot, fig.cap="Weekly SCL-90-R depression subscale (average item score) over the course of the study. The dashed line is the linear time trend estimated from the weekly assessments."}
```

# Model

A simple linear model estimates the time trend of the weekly depression ratings
across **all** phases of the study. It tests only the linear component of
change over time.

```{r model}
```

Save the fitted model and the figure for use elsewhere (e.g., the manuscript):

```{r save}
```

# Reporting results with `cocoon`

The `cocoon` package formats model statistics so that they can be embedded
directly into text. `format_stats(model)` returns a formatted string for the
whole model; with `term`, the output is restricted to one term.

## Whole-model statistics

```{r format-model, results="asis"}
cat(cocoon::format_stats(model))
```

## Statistics for a single term

```{r format-term, results="asis"}
cat(cocoon::format_stats(model, term = "week"))
```

## Inline use in running text

The sentence below is written in R Markdown as
``Depression ratings changed linearly over time (`r knitr::inline_expr('cocoon::format_stats(model, term = "week")')`).``
and renders as:

> Depression ratings changed linearly over time
> (`r cocoon::format_stats(model, term = "week")`).

The overall fit can be reported likewise: `r cocoon::format_stats(model)`.

If the data, the code in `R/analysis.R`, or the model change, re-running
`make all DOCKER=TRUE` updates the figure, the output, and every number in the
text.
